events.description: Baseline before the stroke: independent, history of PFO, superficial venous thrombi and depression, former smoker, home medications

evidence.quote: Prior to the cerebellar CVA, the patient was active and independent with both basic and advanced activities of daily living (ADL).
Her health history included a patent foramen ovale, two superficial venous thrombi, and a history of depression.
Prior to admission, her medications included aspirin 81 mg daily, estradiol 0.5 mg, ibuprofen 200 mg, a daily multivitamin, nystatin suspension, and 500 mg of vitamin C.

events.description: Emergency center presentation with dizziness, severe headache, diaphoresis, photophobia, nausea and emesis after being unable to lift herself during pushups

evidence.quote: A 51-year-old healthy female arrived at the emergency center presenting with acute dizziness, a severe headache, diaphoresis, diffuse photophobia, nausea, and emesis.
The patient reported that she had been doing pushups during a televised total body workout and was suddenly unable to lift herself up.

events.description: Initial head CT with no acute intracranial event; bradycardia; symptoms initially believed vasovagal

evidence.quote: A head computerized tomography (CT) demonstrated that there was no acute intracranial event.
Her symptoms were initially believed to be a vasovagal reaction.
She was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.

events.description: Emergency room plan to monitor orthostatic vital signs and hydrate overnight

evidence.quote: The emergency room plan was to monitor orthostatic vital signs and aggressively hydrate overnight.

events.description: Repeat head CT showing acute left cerebellar ischemia; admission with acute cerebellar CVA

evidence.quote: The next day a repeat head CT demonstrated acute ischemia of the left cerebellum mainly in the PICA distribution.
Upon this finding, the patient was admitted into the hospital diagnosed with an acute cerebrovascular accident (CVA) in the cerebellum.

events.description: Initial SLP, PT and OT evaluation with NIHSS, modified Rankin and examination findings; stroke protocol

evidence.quote: She was found to have double vision, dizziness when sitting up, and complained of a headache that she subjectively rated as a 7/10 (0 = no pain and 10 = worst pain).
She demonstrated an initial score of three on the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale and was placed on the hospital stroke protocol.
The patient scored a 2/6 (0=no impairment, 6=severe disability/bedridden) on the modified Rankin scale.

events.description: Found face down in the bathroom; head CT with hydrocephalus and brain stem compression; increasing lethargy

evidence.quote: Four days after her admission, she was found face down in bathroom after ambulating there independently.

A head CT revealed hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral ventricles including temporal horns and third ventricle, along with fourth ventricle compression and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

events.description: Transfer to the ICU and emergency left suboccipital craniotomy with removal of infarcted cerebellar areas

evidence.quote: The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) and had emergency surgery for a left suboccipital craniotomy with removal of the infarcted areas in the cerebellum.

events.description: Post-surgical head CT with new hemorrhage, gas in the operative cavity, effaced fourth ventricle and moderate obstructive hydrocephalus

evidence.quote: After surgery, a head CT demonstrated a new hemorrhage and gas within the operative cavity along with an increased mass effect on the left side of the fourth ventricle which was completely effaced with moderate obstructive hydrocephalus.

events.description: Reduced level of consciousness and return to the operating room for right frontal ventriculostomy

evidence.quote: Later in the day the patient demonstrated a reduced level of consciousness and was taken to the operating room again where a right frontal ventriculostomy was performed to decrease the hydrocephalus.

events.description: Posterior fossa decompression and overall poor prognosis

evidence.quote: She subsequently had a posterior fossa decompression and she was deemed to have an overall poor prognosis.

events.description: Remained intubated and unresponsive; elevated ICP; external ventricular drain placed
events.time_text: Three days after her fall and subsequent surgeries

evidence.quote: Three days after her fall and subsequent surgeries, the patient remained orally intubated and unresponsive.
The patient’s intracranial pressure (ICP) was found to be elevated and she had an external ventricular drain (EVD) placed for therapeutic drainage of her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

events.description: Hemorrhage surrounding the EVD in the right frontal lobe and within the right lateral ventricle

evidence.quote: She subsequently developed a hemorrhage surrounding her EVD in the right frontal lobe and a hemorrhage within the right lateral ventricle.

events.description: Surgery to reopen the suboccipital craniotomy for clot evacuation

evidence.quote: The next day she underwent surgery to reopen her suboccipital craniotomy for evacuation of a clot.

events.description: Remained intubated and on a ventilator, medically more stable but verbally unresponsive with positive left Babinski sign
events.time_text: Seven days after her fall and surgery

evidence.quote: Seven days after her fall and surgery, she remained intubated and on a ventilator.
By this time, her medical status became more stable overall, however she remained verbally unresponsive and demonstrated a positive Babinski sign on the left foot.

events.description: Palliative care consultation for care coordination and decision making
events.time_text: 11 days after her fall and surgery

evidence.quote: In light of her poor prognosis, the patient received a palliative care consultation to assist in coordinating care and decision making 11 days after her fall and surgery.

events.description: Tracheostomy completed with ongoing ventilator support
events.time_text: Twelve days after her initial fall

evidence.quote: Twelve days after her initial fall, a tracheostomy was completed and she remained on ventilator support.

events.description: Transfer from ventilator to supplemental oxygen at 28% FiO_(2) via tracheostomy collar

evidence.quote: Two days after the tracheostomy, she was successfully transferred to supplemental oxygen at 28% FiO_(2) via a tracheostomy collar.

events.description: ICU occupational therapy evaluation: minimally responsive, flaccid, dependent; goals set
events.time_text: Three days after the initial fall and surgery

evidence.quote: Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Three days after the initial fall and surgery, the patient was evaluated by OT.

Initially she presented as minimally responsive with her eyes closed throughout the session; she was non-verbal with no attempts to communicate and was flaccid in both arms and legs with mild edema, and dependent with all ADL and functional mobility.

events.description: ICU OT course: multimodal sensory stimulation, bed mobility and ADL retraining, neuromuscular re-education, devices; status in last week and at ICU discharge

evidence.quote: The majority of the ICU OT treatment sessions consisted of MSS, which is an application of a series of sensory techniques that are customized in occurrence and amount in order to increase arousal and awareness to elicit a purposeful behavior.

In the last week of the patient’s stay in the ICU, she demonstrated moderate to maximal assistance with grooming, she was dependent with dressing and toileting, required maximal assistance with side-to-side bed mobility and supine-to-sit transfers, and continued to have poor static and dynamic seated balance.

At discharge from the ICU, her alertness improved and she displayed consistent command following and was progressing to using one or two fingers and head motions for no/yes with good accuracy and she was consistently alert and oriented to one to two.

events.description: ICU physical therapy initiated: passive range of motion, early mobility, tilt table
events.time_text: 30 days after the patient’s initial fall

evidence.quote: Physical therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Physical therapy treatments were initiated 30 days after the patient’s initial fall and eight days after OT was initiated in the ICU.
At week five, the tilt table was introduced with intervals of two to ten minute holds to allow her vitals and symptoms to stabilize.

events.description: Six-week ICU stay with OT, PT, SLP visits and restorative aide services

evidence.quote: The patient was in the ICU for a total of six weeks and received 19 visits of OT, 12 visits of PT, and 17 visits of SLP.

The patient underwent a total of 14 months of PT and OT – six weeks in the intensive Care Unit (ICU), approximately 10 weeks in Inpatient Rehabilitation (IPR), and 41 weeks of outpatient rehabilitation.

events.description: Direct admission to the inpatient rehabilitation unit for about 10 weeks
events.time_text: after a six week ICU stay

evidence.quote: The patient was directly admitted to the IPR unit after a six week ICU stay.
During inpatient rehabilitation, the patient received a total of 54 visits of OT, 51 visits of PT, 47 visits of SLP and 22 visits of recreation therapy.

events.description: IPR admission OT and PT evaluation: strength, tone, ataxia, assistance levels, devices

evidence.quote: Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: The OT evaluation found decreased muscle strength grossly to both shoulders at 1/5, elbow and wrist strength was 2/5, while the forearm and hands were 3-/5.

Physical therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: The patient’s lower extremity muscle strength via manual muscle testing on initial admission into IPR was 2-/5 for hip flexors while knee extensors, knee flexors and dorsiflexors were 3/5.

events.description: IPR course: sitting balance, transfers, wheelchair propulsion and gait training with unweighting systems, vision treatments

evidence.quote: By week four in IPR, the patient demonstrated improvement in bed mobility from maximum to moderate assist with improved motor control.

By week six, the patient was able to propel the wheelchair 30 feet utilizing only her legs for propulsion as she was unable to grasp or elevate her upper extremities to the propulsion level of the wheelchair at this point; this improved to 50 feet by week seven of IPR.

By week six, the patient was performing gait training with the SARA Plus walking sling for distances up to 366 m (1,200 ft) with three standing rest breaks with moderate assist with 0-11 kg (0-25 lbs) of unweighting at 0.22 m/s (0.5 mph).
By week nine, the patient was safe enough to perform gait training with one person assistance without a wheelchair following her.

events.description: End of inpatient rehabilitation: status at last week and discharge, discharge home with adaptations

evidence.quote: During her last week in inpatient rehabilitation, she displayed active left shoulder elevation of 110° and 140° on the right and gross left arm strength of 3/5 while the right arm was grossly 3+/5.
Upon discharge from IPR, the patient was sidestepping in the parallel bars 9 m (30 ft) for two repetitions with moderate assistance.
By week 10, the patient could perform daily bathing, grooming, showering, and functional mobility tasks with moderate assistance from her husband without cues from the therapists.

events.time_text: Upon initiation of outpatient PT and OT seventeen weeks after her fall and craniotomy surgery

events.description: Initial outpatient OT interventions and findings

evidence.quote: Occupational therapy evaluation, interventions and outcomes: Occupational therapy was initiated three times a week for 45 to 60 minutes per session.

Her OT intervention initially focused on family education for home exercise program (HEP), core stability activities while laying supine on a mat with moderate to maximal assist, and unsupported sitting with moderate assistance.

events.description: Outpatient OT months two and three: fine motor coordination, resisted exercise and re-evaluation

evidence.quote: By the second month, fine motor coordination (FMC) activities were initiated utilizing large sized pegs and beads requiring hand-over-hand assistance for fine motor tasks to facilitate normalized movement patterns secondary to ataxia (Table 3).

During the third month, a resisted upper extremity exercise program was initiated with medium resistance elastic band with scapular retraction and shoulder horizontal abduction/adduction with trunk rotation to strengthen her core.

A re-evaluation was completed after the third month which provided evidence of an increase in control and strength for completion of modified ADLs and transfers with minimal to moderate assistance with perturbations 50% of the time.

events.description: Outpatient OT months four and five: core stability gains and coordination training

events.description: Outpatient OT from six months: self-care independence, feeding tube no longer needed, adaptive techniques
events.time_text: By six months after initiation of outpatient OT

events.description: Outpatient PT months four to ten: PASS 28/36, Berg, gait training, U-step walker

evidence.quote: At four months, her PASS score was 28/36 and was not repeated after this date.

At the beginning of month five, the patient’s Berg balance score was 13/56 (56 = normal balance) and by the end of the sixth month, it had improved to 17/56 and was no longer reported in the medical record.
By month seven, the patient was started on a U-step walker (In-Step Mobility Products, Skokie, IL, 60076. www.ustep.com) to aid in ambulatory control and balance.

events.description: By month ten: plateau of functional level, outcomes and independence at wheelchair level

Overall she progressed in her independence for both basic and advanced ADL and transfers.

summary.text: A 51-year-old previously healthy, athletic female with a patent foramen ovale, two superficial venous thrombi and a history of depression presented with acute dizziness, severe headache, diaphoresis, photophobia, nausea and emesis after being unable to lift herself during pushups. An initial head CT showed no acute intracranial event, symptoms were first believed vasovagal, and she was bradycardic at 25 to 39 beats per minute.

A repeat head CT the next day showed acute left cerebellar ischemia in the PICA distribution and she was admitted with an acute cerebellar CVA, with an initial NIHSS score of three and modified Rankin score of 2/6. Four days after admission she was found face down in the bathroom, and head CT showed hydrocephalus with fourth ventricle and brain stem compression due to edema of a left cerebellar infarct.

She was moved to the ICU for emergency left suboccipital craniotomy with removal of infarcted cerebellar areas, followed by a right frontal ventriculostomy, posterior fossa decompression, an external ventricular drain and reopening of the craniotomy for clot evacuation after new hemorrhages. Judged to have a poor prognosis, she received a palliative care consultation and a tracheostomy, and was moved to a tracheostomy collar with supplemental oxygen.

During about six weeks in the ICU, OT began with multimodal sensory stimulation and PT with early mobility and tilt-table work. After about 10 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, with gains in sitting balance, transfers, wheelchair propulsion and gait training using unweighting systems, she was discharged home with moderate assistance from her husband, a wheelchair, platform walker, shower chair and tub transfer bench.

Outpatient PT and OT lasted 41 weeks, starting with whole body ataxia, weakness, a PEG tube and left eye patching, and PSFS, hand function, PASS, Berg and Timed Up and Go measures were tracked. By month ten she plateaued and functioned at the wheelchair level with family supervision; at 14 months she lived at home with her husband, could ambulate and stand with assistance, and performed most ADL with standby or set-up assistance.
